patient.name: Terrence Walsh
patient.complaint: Four days of productive cough, fever and right-sided chest pain on breathing in

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' or 'most likely organism' with cough, fever, crackles and bronchial breathing; a drinker with bad teeth and foul sputum points to lung abscess.

points: Four days of cough with **green sputum** and fevers.
Sharp right chest pain when he breathes in (**pleuritic**).
More breathless than usual; tired and off his food.

steps.lead: Terrence has a **lower** respiratory tract infection: the bronchi or the lung itself. The question is bronchitis or pneumonia.
His **smoking and COPD** put him at risk, and **Streptococcus pneumoniae** is the bug to bet on.

points: **Bronchial breath sounds** over the same area.
Dull to percussion at the right base.

steps.lead: Crackles fit any LRTI, but Terrence's **bronchial breathing** says the lung itself is involved: **pneumonia**.

steps.q: Which examination finding most suggests pneumonia rather than acute bronchitis?
steps.r: **Bronchial breathing** means consolidated lung. Cough, fever and wheeze happen in bronchitis too.

steps.title: Acute bronchitis vs pneumonia vs lung abscess
head: Feature
Acute bronchitis
Pneumonia
Lung abscess

steps.lead: Terrence is hypoxic at 91%: an **emergency feature**, so he is admitted. Watch for effusion, sepsis and respiratory failure.

steps.text: Foul-smelling sputum in a heavy drinker with bad teeth is not 'just pneumonia'. Think **lung abscess** from aspirated anaerobes.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (chest X-ray showing consolidation) after a vignette where chest examination already found crackles.

steps.lead: The bedside step came first: Terrence's chest examination found the **crackles and bronchial breathing**.

steps.q: What confirms that Terrence has pneumonia?
steps.r: A **chest X-ray showing consolidation** is the diagnostic test. Cultures find the organism, not the diagnosis.

visual.title: Terrence's chest X-ray
visual.caption: Right lower zone consolidation: pneumonia confirmed.

steps.text: The patch matches where you heard the bronchial breathing.

steps.lead: Terrence's film shows **consolidation**: this is what turns 'LRTI' into pneumonia.

steps.title: Admission bloods
steps.text: Neutrophilia and high CRP fit bacterial infection. **Urea above 7** scores a CURB-65 point.

visual.title: CURB-65
visual.label: Terrence 2
visual.caption: Age 65 or over (1) and urea above 7 (1). Not confused, RR under 30, BP fine.

steps.text: CURB-65: **C**onfusion, **U**rea >7 mmol/L, **R**R ≥30, **B**P systolic <90 or diastolic ≤60, age **65** or over. One point each.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' where severity (CURB-65) and penicillin allergy decide the antibiotic.

steps.lead: Terrence's antibiotic follows his **CURB-65 of 2**: moderate severity under the NICE/BTS approach.

steps.title: Severity decides the antibiotic
steps.caption: Clarithromycin is added to cover atypical organisms once disease is moderate or worse.

steps.lead: If Terrence scored 0 to 1 he would go home on **amoxicillin**; doxycycline or clarithromycin if penicillin allergic.

steps.q: Terrence scores CURB-65 2 and has no allergies. Which regimen?
steps.r: Moderate disease: **amoxicillin plus clarithromycin**. Co-amoxiclav plus clarithromycin is kept for severe (3 to 5).

steps.lead: Terrence is **moderate**: amoxicillin plus clarithromycin. If he became confused or hypotensive, escalate to **co-amoxiclav plus clarithromycin**.
He also gets **paracetamol**, fluids and **oxygen** for his 91% saturations (target 88 to 92% with his COPD).

visual.title: Terrence on antibiotics
visual.caption: CRP often peaks on day 1, then falls; afebrile by day 3 means the antibiotic is working.

steps.text: Do not jump to co-amoxiclav for every admission. Match the antibiotic to **severity**: mild, moderate or severe.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why consolidation gives bronchial breathing, why S. pneumoniae is so common, or why aspiration of oral anaerobes forms an abscess.

steps.lead: Terrence's alveoli are filled with **inflammatory exudate**: that is the consolidation on his X-ray and the crackles you heard.

steps.title: From exudate to bronchial breathing
nodes: Neutrophils and fluid flood the air spaces
Solid lung conducts airway sound well
Harsh bronchial breathing over the area

steps.lead: Terrence's pneumococcus probably **colonised his nasopharynx** first, then descended when his COPD and smoking weakened his defences.
Terrence does not have an abscess. A drinker who **aspirates** anaerobic mouth flora, worse with **poor dentition**, would.

steps.q: Which is the main reason poor dentition increases lung abscess risk?
o: Bigger load of anaerobic oral bacteria to aspirate
steps.r: Bad teeth carry more **anaerobes**; impaired consciousness (alcohol) lets them be aspirated.

visual.title: For comparison: lung abscess
visual.caption: A thick-walled cavity, often with an air-fluid level, in a dependent segment after aspiration.

mcq.q: What is the most common bacterial cause of LRTI?
mcq.r: **Streptococcus pneumoniae** is the commonest bacterial cause.

mcq.q: Which sign suggests pneumonia rather than bronchitis?
mcq.r: **Bronchial breathing** means consolidation, so the parenchyma is involved.

mcq.q: Which organisms classically cause lung abscess?
Which pair of risk factors predisposes to lung abscess?
mcq.r: Alcohol impairs consciousness and swallowing; bad teeth add anaerobes.

mcq.q: What is the gold-standard investigation for LRTI?
Mild LRTI in a penicillin-allergic patient?

mcq.r: Severe: **co-amoxiclav plus clarithromycin**. Moderate is amoxicillin plus clarithromycin.

mcq.q: Where does S. pneumoniae live before causing LRTI?
What fills the alveoli in pneumonia?
mcq.r: **Inflammatory exudate** gives consolidation, crackles and bronchial breathing.

technique.stem: A 72 year old man has a 3 day history of cough productive of rusty sputum, fever and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day. On examination there are crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right base. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air.
technique.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?

steps.x: An organism question: decide the diagnosis, then the commonest bug for it.
Productive cough, pleuritic pain and **bronchial breathing**: community-acquired pneumonia. Rusty sputum is classic pneumococcus.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Commonest bacterial cause of LRTI: **Streptococcus pneumoniae**.

elim: Common in COPD exacerbations, but not the commonest cause of pneumonia.
Needs a clue: travel, air conditioning, hyponatraemia, diarrhoea.
Bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis or hospital-acquired infection.
Follows influenza or IV drug use; cavitating pneumonia.

steps.x: **E. Streptococcus pneumoniae.** No special clue = pneumococcus.

technique.stem: A 58 year old woman has a 4 day history of productive cough, fever and breathlessness. On examination there are coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds in the left lower zone. Her temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 124/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: Diagnostic investigation: name the diagnosis, then the test that confirms it.

clues: bronchial breath sounds in the left lower zone
steps.x: Bronchial breathing in one zone = suspected **pneumonia**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A **chest X-ray** showing consolidation confirms it.

elim: Identify the organism in severe disease; they do not diagnose pneumonia.
For suspected PE; fever, sputum and focal signs point to infection.
For asthma or COPD when well, not acute infection.
Guides antibiotics; does not confirm consolidation.

steps.x: **B. Chest X-ray.** Consolidation on CXR = pneumonia.

technique.stem: A 45 year old man has a 3 day history of productive cough and fever. He has a penicillin allergy (anaphylaxis). Crackles are heard at the right base. His temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 92 bpm, BP 128/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. He is alert and his urea is 4.8 mmol/L. A chest X-ray shows right lower zone consolidation.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: No antibiotics and review in 1 week

steps.x: Initial management: work out severity, then check allergies.
CURB-65 = 0 (under 65, not confused, normal urea, RR and BP): **mild** pneumonia, but penicillin allergic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Mild disease would be amoxicillin; with penicillin allergy use **doxycycline** (or clarithromycin).

elim: Severe-disease regimen, and a penicillin.
Consolidation on CXR is bacterial pneumonia: treat it.
A penicillin: dangerous with anaphylaxis.
Also contains a penicillin.

steps.x: **E. Oral doxycycline.** Mild + penicillin allergy = doxycycline or clarithromycin.

technique.stem: A 52 year old man with alcohol dependence has a 3 week history of cough productive of foul-smelling sputum, night sweats and weight loss. He has very poor dentition. A chest X-ray shows a thick-walled cavity with an air-fluid level in the right lung.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism for this condition?
o: Malignant necrosis of a bronchial tumour

steps.x: A mechanism question: name the condition first, then how it forms.

clues: thick-walled cavity with an air-fluid level
steps.x: Drinker, bad teeth, foul sputum, cavity with fluid level: **lung abscess**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Impaired consciousness lets him **aspirate anaerobic mouth flora**, which necrose lung and wall off into a pus cavity.

elim: Gives multiple septic emboli, usually in IV drug users with a murmur.
Possible cavity, but foul sputum and bad teeth point to aspiration.
TB cavities are apical, and sputum is not foul-smelling.
Predisposes to bacterial pneumonia, not anaerobic abscess.

steps.x: **A. Aspiration of anaerobic oral flora.** Foul sputum + alcohol + bad teeth = aspiration abscess.

practice.stem: A 66 year old woman with COPD has a 5 day history of productive cough, fever and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. On examination there are crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the left base. Her temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 106 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Focal crackles with bronchial breathing, fever and pleuritic pain mean consolidation: pneumonia. An exacerbation of COPD gives wheeze, not focal bronchial breathing.

steps.x: Diagnosis: is the lung parenchyma involved?

clues: bronchial breath sounds at the left base
steps.x: Fever, pleuritic pain, high CRP and **bronchial breathing** at one base.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Consolidation: **community-acquired pneumonia**.

elim: No bronchial breathing; bronchitis spares the parenchyma.
Wheeze and sputum, but focal bronchial breathing means pneumonia.
Pleuritic pain, but not fever with purulent cough and focal signs.
Reduced breath sounds and hyper-resonance, not bronchial breathing.

steps.x: **B. Community-acquired pneumonia.** Bronchial breathing = consolidation.

practice.stem: A 48 year old man with alcohol dependence has a 2 week history of cough productive of foul-smelling sputum and fevers. He was found drunk and unresponsive at home 3 weeks ago. He has several decayed teeth. There are coarse crackles over the right upper zone. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. A chest X-ray is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Thick-walled cavity with an air-fluid level, right upper zone.

practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Aspiration while unconscious, poor dentition and foul sputum with a cavity is a lung abscess from anaerobes. TB is not foul-smelling and needs risk factors.

steps.x: Diagnosis with an X-ray: link the history to the cavity.
Aspiration risk + anaerobe load + foul sputum + coarse crackles + cavity.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A complication of LRTI: **lung abscess**.

elim: Chronic daily sputum for years with dilated airways, not a single cavity.
Pus in the pleural space: a pleural collection, not a lung cavity.
Chronic weight loss, night sweats, contacts; sputum not foul.
Can cavitate, but 2 weeks of fever after aspiration fits abscess.

steps.x: **C. Lung abscess.** Foul sputum + alcohol + bad teeth = aspiration abscess.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man has a 3 day history of productive cough and fever. He is now confused and does not know where he is. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 86/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. A chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation.
practice.q: Which is the most likely CURB-65 severity?
practice.e: He scores for confusion, urea above 7, RR 30 or more, low BP and age 65 or over: 5, severe pneumonia. Needs urgent admission and high-dose antibiotics.

steps.x: A severity question: count the CURB-65 points one by one.
Confusion (1), urea 11.2 (1), RR 32 (1), systolic 86 (1), age 74 (1).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Score **5**: severe.

elim: Every criterion is positive.
Far more than one point.
Ignores confusion, RR and BP.
Undercounts: all five criteria are met.

steps.x: **E. Severe (score 5).** C, U, R, B and 65 all present.

practice.stem: A 61 year old woman is on day 4 of oral amoxicillin and clarithromycin for right lower lobe pneumonia. She still has fevers and more breathlessness. The right base is stony dull to percussion with reduced breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance. Her temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 126/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely complication?
practice.e: Stony dullness with reduced breath sounds and vocal resonance is fluid: a pleural effusion complicating pneumonia (it may be an empyema if fevers persist). Pneumothorax is hyper-resonant.

steps.x: A complication question: what do the new signs mean?
Stony dull + reduced breath sounds + reduced vocal resonance = **fluid**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pleural effusion** complicating her pneumonia.

elim: A chronic condition with daily sputum, not a new dull base.
Coarse crackles and foul sputum; no stony dullness.
Hyper-resonant, not stony dull.
Chronic fine bibasal crackles, not dullness.

steps.x: **C. Parapneumonic pleural effusion.** Stony dull = fluid.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has a 3 day history of cough productive of green sputum, fever and breathlessness. He has COPD. His temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 100 bpm, BP 134/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. A chest X-ray shows left lower zone consolidation.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on chest examination?
o: Absent breath sounds with tracheal deviation away
Fine end-inspiratory crackles at both bases
Stony dullness with reduced vocal resonance
practice.e: Consolidated lung conducts sound well, giving bronchial breathing, and exudate gives crackles. Stony dullness is effusion; hyper-resonance is pneumothorax.

steps.x: A finding question: diagnose first, then predict the sign.
Consolidation on CXR = pneumonia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Consolidation gives focal **crackles and bronchial breathing**.

elim: Tension pneumothorax or massive effusion.
Pulmonary fibrosis.
Pneumothorax.
Pleural effusion; consolidation increases vocal resonance.

steps.x: **B. Bronchial breath sounds and crackles.** The classic sign of consolidation.

practice.stem: A 56 year old woman has a 4 day history of productive cough, fever and pleuritic chest pain. A chest X-ray shows right middle lobe consolidation. She has COPD, smokes 25 cigarettes a day, takes amlodipine for hypertension and has hypothyroidism. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 138/86 mmHg.
practice.q: Which feature of her history most increases her risk of this condition?
practice.e: Smoking (and her COPD) impairs mucociliary clearance and is a key risk factor for LRTI, along with immunosuppression. The other features are distractors.

steps.x: A risk factor question about LRTI.
Pneumonia in a smoker with COPD.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Smoking** is the risk factor in the list (COPD and immunosuppression are the others).

elim: Causes ankle swelling, not chest infection.
Not a risk factor.
Not a risk factor for LRTI.
A distractor; not linked to pneumonia.

steps.x: **E. Smoking.** LRTI risk: smoking, COPD, immunosuppression.

practice.stem: A 63 year old man has a 3 day history of cough productive of yellow sputum and fever. On examination there are crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right base. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 128/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. A chest X-ray is shown (see item resources).
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on the chest X-ray?
o: Consolidation in the right lower zone
Meniscus-shaped opacity at the left base
Visible lung edge with absent markings
practice.e: Bronchial breathing at the right base predicts right lower zone consolidation, which confirms pneumonia. A meniscus is effusion; a lung edge is pneumothorax.

steps.x: An X-ray finding question: match the film to the signs.

clues: bronchial breath sounds at the right base
steps.x: Focal bronchial breathing on the right = consolidation there.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Right lower zone consolidation**: the gold-standard confirmation.

elim: Sarcoidosis or lymphoma.
Lung abscess; no foul sputum or aspiration history.
Effusion, and on the wrong side.
Pneumothorax.

steps.x: **C. Consolidation in the right lower zone.** CXR consolidation confirms pneumonia.

practice.stem: A 34 year old woman attends her GP with a 4 day history of cough productive of green sputum and a temperature of 38.0°C. She feels breathless on stairs. Her pulse rate is 94 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. She is otherwise well.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: Examining the chest for crackles and bronchial breathing is the key first step; it decides whether pneumonia is likely and an X-ray is needed. CT and D-dimer are not first-line.

steps.x: 'Initial' investigation: what do you do first at the bedside?
A well woman with an LRTI picture; bronchitis or pneumonia?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Chest examination** first, looking for crackles and bronchial breath sounds.

elim: Not a first-line test for LRTI.
For suspected VTE; this is infection.
For asthma, not acute infection.
Not routine for a well patient in primary care.

steps.x: **A. Chest examination.** Signs decide the next step.

practice.stem: A 42 year old man has a 3 day history of productive cough and fever. He has no allergies. He is alert. Crackles are heard at the left base. His temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 90 bpm, BP 126/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. A chest X-ray shows left lower zone consolidation.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: CURB-65 is 0, so this is mild pneumonia treated with oral amoxicillin. Doxycycline is for penicillin allergy; dual therapy is for moderate or severe disease.

steps.x: Initial management: score severity, then check allergies.
Not confused, urea normal, RR under 30, BP normal, age 42: CURB-65 **0**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Mild, no allergy: **oral amoxicillin**.

elim: Severe (3 to 5) regimen.
Hospital-acquired or neutropenic sepsis, not mild CAP.
Moderate (CURB-65 2) regimen.
Only if penicillin allergic.

steps.x: **C. Oral amoxicillin.** Mild = amoxicillin.

practice.stem: A 79 year old woman has a 2 day history of productive cough, fever and new confusion. She has no allergies. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 88/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% on 2 L oxygen. A chest X-ray shows left lower lobe consolidation.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?
practice.e: Confusion, urea above 7, low BP and age give CURB-65 4: severe pneumonia, so co-amoxiclav plus clarithromycin. Amoxicillin plus clarithromycin is the moderate regimen.

steps.x: Antibiotic choice: score CURB-65.
Confusion (1), urea 9.8 (1), RR 28 (0), BP (1), age (1): **4**, severe, and septic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Severe: escalate to **co-amoxiclav plus clarithromycin** (IV).

elim: Mild regimen only.
Moderate regimen; she is severe and shocked.
Mild disease with penicillin allergy.
Mild disease with penicillin allergy.

steps.x: **A. Intravenous co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin.** Severe = co-amoxiclav + clarithromycin.

practice.stem: A 68 year old man is admitted with pneumonia. His CURB-65 score is 2. He has no drug allergies. He is started on the appropriate antibiotics. His temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. He has no history of lung disease.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate additional management?
practice.e: Supportive care is paracetamol for fever, fluids and oxygen for hypoxia (saturations 89%). Steroids and diuretics are not routine.

steps.x: 'Additional' management: the antibiotic is done, so think supportive care.
Hypoxic and febrile; no COPD, so target 94 to 98%.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Oxygen** for hypoxia, **paracetamol** for fever, plus fluids.

elim: He needs fluids; he is febrile and tachycardic.
No fluid overload; would worsen dehydration.
Not routine in pneumonia.
Not routinely recommended for uncomplicated pneumonia.

steps.x: **D. Oxygen and paracetamol.** Supportive: paracetamol, fluids, oxygen if hypoxic.

practice.stem: A 60 year old man has a 3 day history of productive cough and fever. On examination there are bronchial breath sounds and increased vocal resonance over the right lower zone. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg. A chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his bronchial breath sounds?
o: Collapse of a lobe from mucus plugging
Fluid collecting in the pleural space
practice.e: Consolidation replaces alveolar air with exudate; the solid lung transmits airway sound, giving bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance. Pleural fluid or air muffles sound.

steps.x: A mechanism question: explain the sign.
Both signs mean sound is conducted better than usual: solid lung.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Alveoli filled with inflammatory exudate** around patent airways.

elim: Pneumothorax reduces breath sounds.
Gives wheeze, not bronchial breathing.
Blocked airway reduces breath sounds.
Effusion reduces breath sounds and vocal resonance.

steps.x: **B. Alveoli filled with inflammatory exudate.** Exudate = consolidation = bronchial breathing.

prompts.q: What is an LRTI, and what is the commonest bacterial cause?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the two main types and the default bug.

points.p: Infection of the bronchi or lungs (acute bronchitis and pneumonia)
points.why: Bronchitis spares the parenchyma; pneumonia does not.
Most acute bronchitis is viral.

points.p: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the commonest bacterial cause
points.why: With no special clue in the stem, the bug is pneumococcus.

prompts.q: Who is at risk of LRTI?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem hides a smoker or someone immunosuppressed.

points.why: Impairs mucociliary clearance.
Damaged airways are easily colonised.
Widens the range of organisms.

prompts.q: Describe the classic presentation and examination findings of an LRTI.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: separate the symptoms from the sign that means pneumonia.

points.why: Rusty sputum classically means pneumococcus.
Systemic upset is commoner in pneumonia.
Pleuritic pain means the pleura over the pneumonia is inflamed.
Occur in both bronchitis and pneumonia.
This is the sign that separates pneumonia from bronchitis.
Hypoxia is an emergency feature.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: new dullness or a cavity on day 4 is a complication question.

points.why: Watch the oxygen in COPD.
Low BP and high lactate: severe.
Stony dull base with ongoing fever.

points.why: These are the emergency features in the notes.

prompts.q: What is a lung abscess, who gets it and how does it present?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: foul sputum + alcohol + bad teeth.

points.p: Necrosis of lung parenchyma forming a pus-filled cavity
points.why: The CXR shows a cavity with an air-fluid level.
Aspiration happens with reduced consciousness.

points.p: Risk factors: alcohol dependence and poor dentition
points.why: Both appear together in the classic stem.
Foul sputum is the giveaway.

prompts.q: What is the first step and the gold-standard investigation for LRTI?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: examine first, then the CXR confirms.

points.p: Chest examination first: crackles and bronchial breath sounds
points.why: The signs decide whether pneumonia is likely.
Cultures identify the bug, not the diagnosis.
Consolidation turns 'LRTI' into pneumonia.

prompts.q: List the CURB-65 criteria and what each score means.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: count the points from the stem, one by one.

points.why: New disorientation in time, place or person.
Look in the Investigations block.
28 does not score.

points.p: BP systolic below 90 or diastolic 60 or less
points.why: Either one scores.
The easy point in older patients.
Severity picks the antibiotic.

prompts.q: Which antibiotic for mild, moderate and severe LRTI, and for penicillin allergy?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: severity first, allergy second.

points.why: Oral at home.
Co-amoxiclav is a penicillin too.
Clarithromycin covers atypicals.
Escalate when CURB-65 is 3 to 5.

prompts.q: What supportive care does a patient with LRTI need?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the 'additional management' after antibiotics.

points.why: Also eases pleuritic pain.
Fever and tachypnoea dehydrate.
Target 88 to 92% if at risk of CO2 retention (COPD).

prompts.q: Why does pneumonia cause crackles and bronchial breathing?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: explain the sign from the pathology.

points.why: Exudate replaces air in the alveoli.

points.p: Solid lung conducts airway sound, giving bronchial breathing
points.why: Effusion and pneumothorax muffle sound instead.

points.p: Crackles come from fluid-filled air spaces opening
points.why: Coarse crackles are louder in abscess.

prompts.q: Why is S. pneumoniae so common, and why does a lung abscess form?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: route of infection explains the risk factors.

points.p: S. pneumoniae colonises the nasopharynx then descends
points.why: Smoking and COPD weaken defences against it.

points.p: Aspirated anaerobic oral flora cause necrotising infection walled off into a cavity
points.why: Dependent segments are hit when lying down.

points.p: Impaired consciousness or swallowing (alcohol) allows aspiration
points.why: Seizures and drug overdose do the same.

points.p: Poor dentition raises the anaerobic load
points.why: More bacteria available to aspirate.

glossary.LRTI: Lower respiratory tract infection: infection of the bronchi or lung tissue below the larynx.
glossary.pneumonia: Infection of the lung parenchyma with alveoli filling with inflammatory exudate.
glossary.acute bronchitis: Inflammation of the bronchi, usually viral, without consolidation of the lung.
glossary.parenchyma: The functional lung tissue: alveoli and their walls, as opposed to airways.
glossary.consolidation: Lung where alveolar air is replaced by fluid or exudate, appearing as white opacity on X-ray.
glossary.crackles: Clicking sounds on inspiration as fluid-filled small airways and alveoli pop open.
glossary.crepitations: Another name for crackles heard with the stethoscope.
glossary.bronchial breath sounds: Harsh, hollow breath sounds with a gap between inspiration and expiration, heard over consolidated lung.
glossary.bronchial breathing: Harsh, hollow breath sounds over consolidated lung, which conducts airway sound well.
glossary.vocal resonance: How clearly speech is heard through the chest wall; increased over consolidation, reduced over fluid.
glossary.pleuritic chest pain: Sharp pain worse on breathing in or coughing, from inflamed pleura.
glossary.stony dull: Very dull percussion note typical of pleural fluid.
glossary.pleural effusion: Fluid collecting between the visceral and parietal pleura.
glossary.empyema: Pus in the pleural space, often complicating pneumonia.
glossary.lung abscess: A pus-filled cavity from necrosis of lung tissue, usually after aspiration of anaerobes.
glossary.anaerobes: Bacteria that grow without oxygen, common in the mouth and dental plaque.
glossary.aspiration: Inhaling mouth or stomach contents into the airways.
glossary.dentition: The condition and arrangement of a person's teeth.
glossary.air-fluid level: A flat line on X-ray where gas sits above fluid inside a cavity.
glossary.Streptococcus pneumoniae: Gram-positive diplococcus; the commonest bacterial cause of community-acquired pneumonia.
glossary.nasopharynx: The upper part of the throat behind the nose.
glossary.atypical organisms: Bacteria such as Mycoplasma and Legionella not covered by penicillins; covered by macrolides.
glossary.CURB-65: Pneumonia severity score: confusion, urea over 7, RR 30 or more, low BP, age 65 or over.
glossary.CAP: Community-acquired pneumonia: pneumonia starting outside hospital.
glossary.COPD: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: fixed airflow obstruction, usually from smoking.
glossary.immunosuppression: Reduced immune defences, e.g. from steroids, chemotherapy or HIV.
glossary.sepsis: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection.
glossary.respiratory failure: Failure of gas exchange: PaO2 below 8 kPa, with or without a raised CO2.
glossary.hypoxia: Low oxygen in the tissues; in practice low saturations or PaO2.
glossary.exudate: Protein-rich inflammatory fluid with cells, leaking from inflamed vessels.
glossary.amoxicillin: Oral penicillin antibiotic; first-line for mild LRTI.
glossary.clarithromycin: Macrolide antibiotic covering atypical organisms; used in moderate and severe LRTI or penicillin allergy.
glossary.doxycycline: Tetracycline antibiotic; alternative for mild LRTI in penicillin allergy.
glossary.co-amoxiclav: Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid; used with clarithromycin in severe LRTI.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein: an inflammatory marker that rises in bacterial infection.
glossary.neutrophilia: Raised neutrophil count, typical of bacterial infection.
